paragraphs: The Author said: Repentance is the return of the servant to his Lord after having turned away from His obedience. God (great and exalted) has made it obligatory upon all who have departed from His commandments and violated His prohibitions, whether ignorantly or knowingly, and He has promised to accept it from whoever turns to Him sincerely and fulfills its conditions. He said (great and exalted): "Return to Me, and I will return to you" (Malachi 3:7), and He said: "If you return to the Lord your God and listen to His voice" (Deuteronomy 4:30), and He said: "And the wicked man, if he turns from all his sins that he has committed and keeps all My statutes and does what is lawful and right, he shall surely live" (Ezekiel 18:21).

God (great and exalted) has opened the gate of repentance wide, and has not closed it so long as the servant lives and his soul is within him. He has said: "As I live, says the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn, turn from your evil ways" (Ezekiel 33:11). And one of the early teachers said: "The gate of repentance is open for every person who wishes to enter through it." This gate is among the greatest gifts God has bestowed upon His creatures, and among the noblest of His mercies — that He has granted the sinner the means to return and to repair, and has not sealed the door against him on account of his transgression.
The Author said: Know, my brother — may God grant you and me success — that departure from God's obedience is of two kinds.

The first is departure from the obligations He has imposed upon us and transgression of the prohibitions He has placed upon us. This is the departure of the wicked from the ways of the righteous, the going of the sinner from the path of God's command.

The second is departure from the full measure of gratitude and devotion owed to God (great and exalted) for His abundant beneficence, His blessings, and His grace. For the righteous and the pious also fall short in this regard, since no one can fulfill the complete obligation of gratitude toward God (great and exalted). The most devoted of servants remains, in truth, unable to repay his Lord for even a single breath of life — and in this sense, even the righteous are penitents of a kind.

Repentance is therefore obligatory upon both types: upon the wicked, to return from sin and transgression; and upon the pious, to return from shortcoming in gratitude and worship, and to renew and redouble their devotion to God (great and exalted).
The Author said: Know that penitents are of three kinds.

The first is one who repents with his tongue alone — speaking words of contrition and asking forgiveness — while his heart remains attached to the sin and his limbs have not ceased from its commission. This person's repentance is invalid and his words are rejected before God, for the heart is the seat of repentance and the origin of all deeds. Of such a person Scripture says: "This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me" (Isaiah 29:13). His repentance is a pretense, and a pretense offered to the One who sees all pretense is a doubled transgression.

The second is one whose heart genuinely grieves and whose limbs have ceased from the sin, but who struggles against his inclinations. When he overcomes them he stands firm in his repentance; when they overpower him he slips and falls back. This person occupies the middle station: his repentance is valid for the time he maintains it, and he requires God's mercy and forgiveness for the moments of his weakness. He is in the condition of the man who has undertaken a sea voyage and must row against a current — the labor is great, and he must not cease rowing for a moment, but with persistence he can arrive.

The third is one who has repented completely — heart, tongue, and limb together — and whose resolution against return to sin is firm and sustained. This is the complete penitent, the one the prophets praised: "When the wicked man turns from his wickedness that he has done and does what is lawful and right, he shall save his soul" (Ezekiel 18:27).
The Author said: Before the servant undertakes repentance, seven things must be established in him.

The first is that he distinguish between the obligatory and the forbidden — for how can one repent of a sin he does not recognize as sin, or fulfill a duty he does not recognize as duty? Ignorance of the law is not a foundation for repentance; it must first be corrected by learning.

The second is that he recognize God's greatness (great and exalted) and His majesty, and understand that his sin is not merely an infraction against a rule but a rebellion against the sovereign of all sovereigns. The magnitude of an offense is measured by the magnitude of the one offended.

The third is that he grasp the severity of his transgression — understanding that no sin against God (great and exalted) is trivial, since God's honor is infinite and the debt incurred by dishonoring Him is proportionately grave.

The fourth is that he recognize the magnitude of God's patience and forbearance with him — that God did not hasten to punish him despite his sins — and understand that this patience is an invitation to repentance, not a license for continued transgression.

The fifth is that he fear punishment: the punishment of this world and of the world to come. This fear must be genuine and grounded in reflection, not a passing feeling, and it must motivate him to flee from sin as one flees from fire.

The sixth is that he hope in God's mercy and His acceptance of the repentant. For without this hope the door of repentance would seem closed and the sinner would despair of return — and despair itself is a sin. Remorse must always be paired with trust.

The seventh is that he grieve over the time he has wasted in disobedience and the moments squandered in heedlessness, recognizing that each day of negligence is a debt that must be repaid and that cannot be fully recovered — though God in His mercy may grant something in its place.
The Author said: The conditions and pillars of repentance — by which a repentance is made complete and valid — are four.

The first is remorse (nadm): genuine sorrow in the heart over the sin committed. This is the root of repentance, and from it all the other pillars derive. For if the heart does not grieve over the sin, none of the other conditions will be present sincerely. The sorrow must be for the sin itself — not merely for its consequences or its exposure — and it must be directed toward the One against whom the sin was committed.

The second is cessation (tark): the complete abandonment of the sin in deed and in intention. So long as the sinner continues the sin even in part, or retains in his heart the intention to return to it, his repentance is invalid. Cessation is the body's portion of repentance, as remorse is the heart's.

The third is confession and supplication for forgiveness (iqrār wa-l-istighfār): acknowledging before God (great and exalted) the sin committed and asking His pardon. This is the tongue's portion of repentance. It must be specific, humble, and sincere, and it must be accompanied by the heart's remorse and the limb's cessation — otherwise it is empty words.

The fourth is the pledge not to return (ḍamān): a firm resolution in the heart never to repeat the sin. This pledge must be sincere and grounded — not a vague hope, but a complete commitment reinforced by whatever practical measures the servant can take to prevent recurrence. Without this pledge, the repentance lacks a future: the other three conditions look backward, to the sin already committed; the pledge looks forward, to the life that begins now.
The Author said: I shall now elaborate the conditions of each pillar in detail, so that the servant may examine himself against each one and know whether his repentance is complete.
**The Conditions of Remorse:**
The first condition of remorse is that it be continuous and persistent, not a momentary feeling that passes with the occasion of sin.

The second is that the sorrow be proportionate to the gravity of the sin — greater grief for greater transgressions, proportionate grief for lesser ones — rather than a uniform emotion indifferent to the nature of the act.
The third is that the grief encompass the sin itself and not merely its consequences: the penitent must grieve that he defied his Creator, not merely that he brought trouble upon himself.

The fourth is that remorse not be accompanied by despair — for despair negates the hope in God's mercy without which no repentance can proceed. Remorse must be paired with trust that forgiveness is possible.
The fifth is that remorse be expressed outwardly in increased piety and good deeds, as visible signs of the inner transformation — for genuine grief over sin radiates outward and alters the life.
**The Conditions of Cessation:**
The first condition of cessation is immediacy: abandonment of the sin must be immediate upon the resolve to repent, not deferred to a more convenient time.
The second is completeness: the sinner must cease from the sin entirely, not merely reduce it. One who repents of theft but continues to steal less than before has not truly ceased.
The third is the removal of occasion: the penitent must distance himself from the circumstances, companions, and environments that enabled the sin.
The fourth is that the penitent not substitute one sin for another, believing that this constitutes repentance. True cessation is from all prohibited acts, not a rearrangement among them.
The fifth is that the cessation be sustained over time — for a cessation subsequently abandoned was not true repentance but a temporary interruption.
**The Conditions of Confession:**

The first condition of confession is that it be directed to God (great and exalted) alone, for it is against Him that all sin is ultimately committed, and it is from Him alone that forgiveness can come.

The second is that the confession be specific: the penitent must acknowledge the particular sin, not cover it in vague generalities that reflect an unwillingness to face the full truth of what was done.
The third is that the confession be made with humility and contrition, not with pride or self-justification or minimization.
The fourth is that the confession be accompanied by a sincere supplication for forgiveness, trusting in God's mercy and accepting His judgment.
The fifth is that the confession not be delayed — for the longer the sinner waits to confess, the more his attachment to the sin deepens and the harder the path of return becomes.
**The Conditions of the Pledge:**
The first condition of the pledge is that it be absolute and unconditional: "I will never return to this" — not "I hope not to return" or "I will try not to return."
The second is that the pledge be supported by practical measures: altering habits, associations, and environment so that the circumstances that led to sin are dismantled.
The third is that the pledge encompass the future entirely — not "I will not return to this sin next week" but "I will not return to this sin in my life."
The fourth is that the pledge be accompanied by constant awareness of God's observation, so that the penitent feels at every moment that his Creator sees him and cannot be deceived.
The fifth is that the pledge be renewed regularly — especially in times of temptation — so that it does not weaken through neglect or fade through forgetfulness.
The Author said: The causes that move the servant toward repentance are four.

The first is hope in God's reward and His promise of forgiveness and of the world to come. When the servant meditates on what God has prepared for the repentant, the desire for that reward draws him toward repentance.
The second is fear of God's punishment — the punishment of this world and of the world to come. When the servant contemplates the severity of retribution for sin, fear drives him to flee it.

The third is gratitude for God's beneficence. When the servant reflects on all that God (great and exalted) has bestowed upon him — life, health, sustenance, intellect, children, provision in every form — shame at his ingratitude moves him to repentance. He has received the greatest of gifts and repaid the giver with disobedience; this recognition, when genuine, is a powerful mover.

The fourth is love of God (great and exalted). This is the highest and most complete cause of repentance. The servant who loves God finds the thought of having displeased Him unbearable — not because he fears punishment, not because he hopes for reward, but because the love itself cannot coexist with estrangement from its object. He who repents from love has attained the highest degree of this gate.

Of these four causes, love is the most noble and most perfect. But the sages have taught that all four are valid paths, appropriate to different souls at different stages of their spiritual development, and none should be despised.
The Author said: Know that there are things which corrupt and invalidate repentance even after it has been genuinely undertaken. I shall enumerate the most important of them.
The first and gravest corruptor is persistence in sin while claiming to have repented. This makes the repentance a lie, and a lie offered to the Omniscient is a doubled transgression.

The second is relapse into the sin after true repentance. A relapse is more grievous than the original sin because it breaks a covenant the penitent established with his Creator. He must then repent again with still greater earnestness, and the second repentance must be more vigorous and more sustained than the first, to compensate for the covenant broken.

The third is the deferral of repentance — saying "I will repent tomorrow" or "I will repent when I am older" or "when this desire is satisfied." This is among the stratagems of the evil inclination, which knows that so long as repentance is deferred, time passes and death may come before the deferral ends. Our early teachers said: "Repent one day before your death" — meaning, since no one knows the day of his death, one must repent every day.

The fourth is partial repentance — repenting of some sins while retaining others. True repentance is a turning of the whole self toward God; the servant who abandons theft but continues in slander has altered his outward conduct in one area while leaving the inner posture of rebellion intact.

The fifth is backbiting and slander committed after repentance — or not repented from. Sins of the tongue that harm others are not forgiven by God until the offended party forgives. They are among the most difficult to repair, for words once spoken cannot be recalled, and the harm they cause spreads beyond the original speaker's reach.

The sixth is having led others to sin. Whoever corrupts others bears their sin alongside his own — their transgressions remain attributed to him until those he corrupted have themselves repented. This is why Scripture says of Jeroboam son of Nevat that he "sinned and caused Israel to sin" — the sins of those he corrupted adhered to him.

The seventh is ingratitude for the very gift of repentance. Repentance is itself a divine grace — the servant who receives it without recognizing it as such has diminished his enjoyment of the gift and placed an obstacle on the path of its continuation.
The Author said: The scholars have debated the relative standing of the penitent and the one who has never sinned. I say they fall into three categories of comparison.

In the first category, the penitent equals the righteous. This is the case when the penitent's repentance is complete in all its conditions and his subsequent life of worship is equal in quality to that of the one who never sinned. Scripture indicates this when it declares that God will forgive the penitent and his former sins will not be recalled against him — as if they had never been. The penitent who achieves this stands before God as one who has been purified to the state of original righteousness.

In the second category, the penitent surpasses the righteous. This is the case when the penitent, having tasted sin and its bitterness, emerges from repentance with a knowledge of transgression's consequences that the one who never sinned cannot possess. His worship is more ardent, his humility deeper, his gratitude more intense, because he knows what he was saved from. Our sages said: "In the place where penitents stand, the perfectly righteous cannot stand." The penitent's path was harder — he overcame what the righteous man was never tested by — and the harder victory produces a stronger character.

In the third category, the righteous surpasses the penitent. This is the case when one regards the life in full: the one who never sinned has maintained his purity throughout, never broken his covenant with God, never required the painful work of restoration. His record is unmarked; the penitent's carries the scar of former transgression even after forgiveness.

Each of these three comparisons is true in its proper context. The wise man will not misuse the second category as license to sin willfully in order to repent "from a higher place" — for willful sin with the intention of later repenting is itself a desecration of the institution of repentance and a deception of the One who cannot be deceived.
The Author said: Sins differ in the difficulty of repentance from them. In general, they fall into two great categories.

The first is sins between man and God alone — commandments neglected, prohibitions violated — in which no other human being is harmed. Repentance from these is entirely a matter between the servant and his Creator. When the servant returns to God with genuine remorse, cessation, confession, and pledge, God's mercy is immediately available, and Scripture's assurances of forgiveness apply in full force.

The second is sins between man and his fellow — theft, fraud, slander, bodily harm, violation of trust. These are far more difficult to repent from, for two reasons: first, because the offended party must be made whole before God's forgiveness is sought; second, because the harm done may be impossible to fully repair. The thief must return what he stole; the slanderer must seek pardon from the one he slandered; the one who caused financial loss must compensate it. Only after making the fullest possible amends to the human victim can the servant turn to God for pardon of his offense against the divine order.

The third category combines both: sins that harm both God and other human beings simultaneously. These are the most demanding, requiring both complete human restitution and complete divine repentance.

The penitent who faces the second or third category must not despair. Even when perfect repair is impossible — the slandered party cannot be found, or the stolen object was consumed — let him do whatever lies in his power and trust in God's mercy for what lies beyond his power. God does not demand the impossible, and He knows what each servant is capable of.

The Author said: I shall now teach certain stratagems by which the servant may help himself to repent from sins most difficult to repent from — those that have become ingrained habits, those whose pleasure runs deepest, and those whose circumstances are most thoroughly embedded in his life.

The first stratagem is regular self-accounting: at a set time each day or each week, reviewing one's deeds and examining one's state. This accounting keeps the servant aware of his spiritual condition and prevents the gradual drift into heedlessness that is the beginning of all ruin.

The second stratagem is the choice of righteous companions. The servant cannot be stronger than his environment; if those around him sin freely, he will be pulled along. Companions who take worship seriously and hold one another to account become a powerful support for repentance and for the maintenance of it.

The third stratagem is the study of the accounts of the righteous and the penitent — reading of their struggles and their triumphs, and drawing from their example both inspiration and practical guidance.

The fourth stratagem is to begin with the commandments and renunciations that are easy, as a foundation for the harder ones. The servant who begins with what he can do strengthens his spiritual capacity for what he previously could not do.

The fifth stratagem is meditation on death and the brevity of life. The servant who genuinely contemplates that he will stand before the Creator and give account of every deed — who truly grasps that the day of death is unknown and may arrive at any moment — is far less likely to waste what remains in heedlessness.

Now, my brother — may God have mercy on you and on me — I have explained to you the obligations of repentance, and I have disclosed to you the means by which you may recover from your shortcomings in the obedience of your Lord, what the argument has established against you, and the excuse has been removed from you. What will you say to your Creator tomorrow when He questions you? Did you not know? But you knew. Did you act in ignorance? But you acted in full knowledge. What then will your answer be to this question? We shall surely be called to account. Prepare the answer while you still have time.

Know, my brother, that the answer to that question comes only from our deeds, not from our words. Therefore have mercy on yourself, that you may reach the pleasure of your Lord — for whoever hastens to the good today will enjoy its fruit, and the fruit of negligence is regret. Awaken, my brother, from the sleep of your heedlessness, and have compassion on yourself — for you are the most precious trust God has placed in your own keeping. How long, and until when, this delay? You have spent your life in the satisfaction of your desires, as the wicked servant does. Will you not reclaim your remaining days in the pleasure of your Lord? You know that life is short and what remains is inevitably shorter still, as our early teachers said: "The day is short and the work is great" (Avot 2:15).

You had, my brother, a high and noble ambition with which you honored this passing world and turned away from your eternal world. Will you not raise your ambition to the more noble place and the loftier station — to which great ambitions are directed forever — and seize the opportunity while the gate of repentance stands open to God, and forgiveness is attainable, and the acceptance of repentance is available? As Scripture says: "Seek the Lord while He may be found; call upon Him while He is near" (Isaiah 55:6).

Hasten then, my brother — hasten — before what you fear descends upon you. For you have no certainty of tomorrow. Look to yourself with the discernment befitting you and the balance your intellect demands. And whoever wishes to reach the pleasure of his Lord, let him enter through the narrow gate through which the patient and the righteous have entered — for none reaches it but those who hasten toward it and race to it, as our early teachers said: "Be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, and strong as a lion to do the will of your Father in Heaven" (Avot 5:20). And the pious one said: "I made haste and did not delay to keep Your commandments" (Psalms 119:60).

Take account of yourself, my brother, and be ashamed before your Creator to deal with Him in a manner you would not accept from a fellow mortal. You know that if you offended even the least important of the king's companions, you would not delay your contrition and your prostration before him seeking his pardon — despite his weakness and powerlessness without God's power. And if the minister angered you, how much more the prince — you would hasten to him with requests for forgiveness and race to him with repentance and apology, fearing the swift arrival of his punishment; and you know his weakness in carrying it out without God's power, as the wise man said: "The heart of a king is like streams of water in the hand of the Lord; He turns it wherever He wishes" (Proverbs 21:1). And you know the swiftness of his reign's passing and its power's end, and his being preoccupied with one matter at the expense of another, and the falling upon him of distraction and forgetfulness, and how much of even the outward appearance of things is hidden from him, let alone their inner reality. With all this knowledge you do not delay hastening to seek pardon for your sin before him. How then are we not ashamed, my brother, before our Creator who is aware of both the inner and the outer of all our deeds and thoughts — upon Whom distraction and forgetfulness cannot fall, Whom nothing distracts from anything, from Whose wisdom there is no escape and Whose reign does not end? How do we turn away from Him and delay returning to Him and repenting before Him, with no knowledge of when our appointed time concludes?

If there were someone to warn the people of a town or city and say: "O people, prepare for the journey to the world to come, for one person among you will be taken in this month, and I do not know who that person is" — would it not be right that every one of them be on guard against death, fearing that he might be the one taken? How much more so when we witness death each month in every direction consuming many of the living — is it not obligatory upon us to fear for ourselves each month, and to examine the state of our provisions and our hereafter before we need them, even if only by a single day? As our early teachers said: "Repent one day before your death" (Avot 2:10). And Scripture says: "At all times let your garments be white" (Ecclesiastes 9:8).

Consider by your faculty of reason and your power of discernment the truth of this, from what you see with your own eyes — more than from what others tell you — and do not resist your intellect and your understanding. And it has been said: God has graces upon His servants; if they accept them, they profit by them, and if they return them to Him, they become arguments against them, then turn to punishments. And God (great and exalted) has blessed you, my brother, with understanding and heart and intellect and knowledge by which you have been distinguished above others. Beware then — beware — lest the blessing of God become an argument against you. He has moved you toward the path of your guidance and alerted you to the way of your correction, with gentleness and compassion, not content that you persist in your heedlessness and continue in your transgression — following the way of His grace, which He is worthy of, and His mercy toward His creatures, as He said: "The Lord is good to all, and His mercies are upon all His works" (Psalms 145:9), and He said: "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore He instructs sinners in the way" (Psalms 25:8).

God has called to you with gentleness and softness, then with reproof and rebuke, then reminded you of punishment that you might return to Him and hasten to repentance before Him. Hasten then — hasten — to heed Him and turn toward Him, and choose for yourself what your Lord has chosen for you, and be content with what your Creator has approved for you, and do not let laziness lead you to scorn yourself — for if you hold yourself cheap, what will you hold dear?

Beware lest the whisper of your heart deceive you and say: "Now, after such long heedlessness and the passing of most of my life, I will repent to God and seek His forgiveness." You must answer it with what the prophet declared: "But when the wicked man turns from his wickedness that he has committed and does what is lawful and right, he shall save his soul" (Ezekiel 18:27), and: "But when the righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity..." to the end of the passage.

Our predecessors compared this to a man who carried purses of silver and needed to cross a great wadi. When he stood at its bank he threw the purses into the water, hoping to stop the current with them — and threw them all in save one remaining with him. But the water was not stopped. When he saw this he said to the boatman at the wadi: "Take this remaining purse and carry me across in your boat." And the boatman did so, and the man arrived at his destination with that one purse, and recouped by it what he had lost of all the other purses he had thrown away — as though nothing had been lost from him.

So too the master of repentance who has spent most of his life in other than the obedience of his Lord: if he recoups this with repentance in the remainder of his time, God will forgive him all that preceded of his ugly deeds throughout his long years, as He said: "None of his transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him" (Ezekiel 18:22), and He said: "None of his sins that he has committed shall be remembered against him" (Ezekiel 18:22).

Let my admonition to you about the neglected account not weigh heavily upon you — for I have not singled you out to the exclusion of myself. Submit to the truth and do not flee from it, and give thanks to God who has alerted you to what you did not know. Do not take your long heedlessness and the heedlessness of those who warn you as an argument and an excuse — for these are among the stratagems of passion and its snares for those who are weak in their discernment.
May God make us and you among those who hasten toward Him and turn toward Him and are sincere before Him — through His mercy and the abundance of His grace. And to Him be praise for that, forever.
